115	                                                                                                                                       Introduction: a self-fulfilling prophecy
116	
117	                                                                                                                                      “We must be careful not to believe things simply because we want them to be true, no
118	                                                                                                                                      one can fool you as easily as you can fool yourself“
119	                                                                                                                                                                                                    Richard Feymann
120	
121	                                                                                                                                      It is tempting to believe a theory when it appears reasonable and it fits with one’s
122	                                                                                                                                      beliefs. For example, the theory that training “too much” or “too little”, or “too much
123	                                                                                                                                      too soon” might cause sports injury seems biologically plausible and aligns well with
124	                                                                                                                                      training dogma. Common beliefs about how training load affects the chances of the
125	                                                                                                                                      athlete getting injured have been strongly shaped by a combination of old and deeply-
126	                                                                                                                                      held training principles, best practice and common sense. Progressive overload, as
127	                                                                                                                                      well as the ‘danger’ of excessive training (overtraining or non-functional
128	                                                                                                                                      overreaching) are well-recognized training principles. The idea that excessive training
129

135	
136	                                                                                                                                      Popular beliefs about training load and injury obfuscate important concepts and
137	                                                                                                                                      methodological issues. Unfortunately, these issues have not been well accounted for
138	                                                                                                                                      in previous research. Our concern is that the training load and injury research field is
139	                                                                                                                                      dominated by well-intentioned, yet potentially misleading, recommendations for
140	                                                                                                                                      clinical practice.
141	
142	                                                                                                                                      Collecting injury and training load data is now considered best practice in sport.14 An
143	                                                                                                                                      unfortunate consequence of such a data rich environment is that researchers studying

170	                                                                                                                                      Clinical question
171	
172	                                                                                                                                      Is the methodological rigour of studies investigating relationships between training
173	                                                                                                                                      load and injury sufficient to inform training load-related decisions in clinical practice?
174	                                                                                                                                      We have highlighted why it is important to critically examine the strength of evidence
175	                                                                                                                                      supporting the claims made in several training load-injury studies.36 In this clinical
176	                                                                                                                                      commentary , we focus on sources of degrees of freedom that can favour questionable
177	                                                                                                                                      research practices (including p-hacking and HARK-ing (Hypothesizing After the
178	                                                                                                                                      Results are Known)) that can impact on the trustworthiness of research findings and
179	                                                                                                                                      the application of training load metrics in clinical practice.

182	                                                                                                                                       A robust conceptual framework: the first step in designing quality research to
183	                                                                                                                                      help clinicians and athletes
184	
185	                                                                                                                                      Developing a conceptual framework is an essential early step when designing
186	                                                                                                                                      research to inform clinical practice. If properly developed, a conceptual framework
187	                                                                                                                                      can guide researchers’ hypotheses and specific research questions, and provide a
188	                                                                                                                                      frame for analyzing data and interpreting the results.34 54 HARK-ing is a bit like doing
189	                                                                                                                                      research in reverse. When (well-intentioned) researchers do not develop a clear
190	                                                                                                                                      conceptual framework before collecting research data, they risk fashioning a
191	                                                                                                                                      hypothesis to suit their research results, and the temptation to conduct (unplanned)
192	                                                                                                                                      analyses until they find something “significant” (p-hacking).
193	
194	                                                                                                                                      There have been attempts within the training load injury field to provide generic

201	                                                                                                                                      nature of injuries and contextual factors that influence injury, but they lack detail to
202	                                                                                                                                      define precise research questions and/or select specific training load metrics. This
203	                                                                                                                                      necessitates the use of plausible biological and physiological rationale to select
204	                                                                                                                                      specific training load measures of exposure as potential prognostic factors for certain
205	                                                                                                                                      injuries. The conceptual framework proposed by Bertelsen et al.,6 is the most
206	                                                                                                                                      appropriate model of the causes of running-related injury (Figure 1).41 While one can
207	                                                                                                                                      argue the suitability of specific proxy measures (e.g. the use of ratios, or 7 and 28
208	                                                                                                                                      days cumulative load), we applaud the authors for transparently presenting their
209	                                                                                                                                      research assumptions, and encourage researchers to consider using the framework6 as

252	
253	                                                                                                                                      Many studies have reported associations between training load and sports injuries.
254	                                                                                                                                      However, the results are inconsistent and often confusing.17 We summarised the
255	                                                                                                                                      results (odd ratio (OR), relative risk (RR), and injury risk) of studies in soccer that

257	                                                                                                                                      Global Positioning System (GPS) measures for non-contact injuries (Figure 2, Figure
258	                                                                                                                                      3). Some studies have reported a relationship between high ACWR and injury, some
259	                                                                                                                                      have reported a relationship between low ACWR and injury, and others have reported
260	                                                                                                                                      no relationship between ACWR and injury.

323	                                                                                                                                      We believe the training load–injury field is at high risk of ‘data fishing’ – where
324	                                                                                                                                      researchers go searching (consciously or unconsciously) for answers in the data to
325	                                                                                                                                      confirm a relationship between training load and injury. Clinicians trying to apply
326	                                                                                                                                      research findings in practice may not be aware of all of the choices researchers must
327	                                                                                                                                      make when conducting a study, and how each choice might influence the results.

341	                                                                                                                                      collected. Because there are so many different measures of training load (exposure),35

366	                                                                                                                                      Measures of exposure are calculated using various training load metrics. However,
367	                                                                                                                                      training load can be assessed using different methods and devices, which further
368	                                                                                                                                      complicates the selection of suitable measures. Again, a conceptual framework
369	                                                                                                                                      should provide guidance when selecting appropriate training load measures.

376	                                                                                                                                      time window within which to measure acute load, and what is an appropriate time
377	                                                                                                                                      window within which to measure chronic load. The original Banister model cannot

386	                                                                                                                                      Typical time lags between injury registration and the acute or chronic load typically
387	                                                                                                                                      range from few days to one week (subsequent week injuries)11 29 31 40 but longer lags
388	                                                                                                                                      have been used.40 59 There is no reason to expect that the training completed on the

390	                                                                                                                                      explain why they chose a particular time lag over another time lag, raising suspicion

440	                                                                                                                                      Correlation does not equal causation
441	
442	                                                                                                                                      The dominant narrative of the training load–injury field is that by manipulating
443	                                                                                                                                      training load, one can alter the probability of future injuries. However, this assumes a
444	                                                                                                                                      cause-effect relationship (changing training load causes an injury to occur or not to

449	                                                                                                                                      causal inferences.20 26 51 52
450	
451	                                                                                                                                      Although the field acknowledged that association is not prediction,19 25 28 48
452	                                                                                                                                      (associations between training load metrics and injury do not automatically imply that
453	                                                                                                                                      training load metric can predict injury occurrence) – it is important to recognize that
454	                                                                                                                                      neither associations nor predictors can be automatically used to make causal
455	                                                                                                                                      inferences if this was not the original aim.27 Associations can be descriptive,
456	                                                                                                                                      predictive or used to estimate causal effects. However, if no causal relationship has
457	                                                                                                                                      been estimated, any practical applications regarding the manipulation of the
458	                                                                                                                                      prognostic factor/predictor to alter the probability of an event is an over interpretation
459	                                                                                                                                      and a speculation (and should be declared as such).

502	                                                                                                                                      this may not be the case for clinicians who may not be as familiar with athletic
503	                                                                                                                                      training methods. Stronger multidisciplinary collaboration may help when making
504	                                                                                                                                      decisions about future training. We recommend clinicians work together with the
505	                                                                                                                                      various support staff of athletes/teams so that any specific knowledge and expertise is
506	                                                                                                                                      shared.
507	
508	                                                                                                                                      When reading research in the training load–injury field, be on the look out for
509	                                                                                                                                      inconsistent results (“consistent” associations but in any direction is not a consistent
510	                                                                                                                                      finding) and different analysis methods that are not well justified (e.g. computational
511	                                                                                                                                      manipulations of the same prognostic factors, data trimming, categorizations, etc).
512	                                                                                                                                      Consider whether the results make sense in the practical context. For example,
