Clinical commentary



                                                                                                                                      Training load and injury: part 2. Questionable research practices hijack the
                                                                                                                                      truth and mislead well-intentioned clinicians


                                                                                                                                      Franco M. Impellizzeri, PhD,1 Patrick Ward, PhD,1, Aaron J. Coutts, PhD,1, Luke
                                                                                                                                      Bornn, PhD,2 Alan McCall, PhD,1,3


                                                                                                                                      1, University of Technology Sydney (UTS), Human Performance Research Centre,
                                                                                                                                      Faculty of Health, Sydney, NSW, Australia




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      2, Strategy and Analytics, Sacramento Kings, Sacramento, California, USA
                                                                                                                                      3, Arsenal Performance and Research Team, Arsenal Football Club, London, UK


                                                                                                                                      Corresponding Author: 37
                                                                                                                                      Professor Franco M Impellizzeri
                                                                                                                                      Human Performance Research Centre, Faculty of Health, University of Technology
                                                                                                                                      Sydney
                                                                                                                                      T. +61 (02) 9514 5204
                                                                                                                                      M. +61 (0) 404 560 633




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      Driver Avenue, Moore Park NSW 2021
                                                                                                                                      PO Box 123. Broadway NSW 2007 Australia


                                                                                                                                      Funding
                                                                                                                                      No funding support has been obtained for the present manuscript.

                                                                                                                                      Financial Disclosure and Conflict of Interest. The Authors affirm that they have no
                                                                                                                                      financial affiliation (including research funding) or involvement with any commercial
                                                                                                                                      organization that has a direct financial interest in any matter included in this




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                      manuscript

                                                                                                                                      Authors’ contribution
                                                                                                                                      All the authors listed have contributed substantially according to ICMJE criteria:
                                                                                                                                      conception of the work in full or some sections, interpretation of published data,
                                                                                                                                      drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content, approved
                                                                                                                                      the final version be submitted and published.

                                                                                                                                      Data sharing
                                                                                                                                      No original data were used for the commentary.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 1
                                                                                                                                       Abstract

                                                                                                                                      Background:
                                                                                                                                      In this clinical commentary, we highlight issues related to conceptual foundations and
                                                                                                                                      methods used in the training load-injury research. We focus on sources of degrees of
                                                                                                                                      freedom that can favour questionable research practices such as p-hacking and
                                                                                                                                      HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known), which can undermine the
                                                                                                                                      trustworthiness of research findings.
                                                                                                                                      Clinical question:
                                                                                                                                      Is the methodological rigour of studies in the training load-injury field sufficient to
                                                                                                                                      inform training-related decisions in clinical practice?
                                                                                                                                      Key findings:
                                                                                                                                      The absence of a clear conceptual framework, causal structure, and reliable methods
                                                                                                                                      can promote questionable research practices, selective reporting and confirmation




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      bias. The fact that well accepted training principles (e.g. overload progression) are in
                                                                                                                                      line with some study findings may simply be a consequence of confirmation bias,
                                                                                                                                      resulting from cherry picking and emphasizing results that align with popular beliefs.
                                                                                                                                      Identifying evidence-based practical applications, grounded in high-quality research is
                                                                                                                                      not currently possible. The strongest recommendation we can make for the clinician is
                                                                                                                                      grounded in common sense “do not train too much too soon” – not because it has been
                                                                                                                                      confirmed by studies, but because it reflects accepted generic training principles.
                                                                                                                                      Clinical application:
                                                                                                                                      The training load-injury research field has fundamental conceptual and
                                                                                                                                      methodological weaknesses. Therefore, making decisions about planning and




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      modifying training programs for injury reduction in clinical practice, based on
                                                                                                                                      available studies, is premature. Clinicians should continue to rely on best practice,
                                                                                                                                      experience and well-known training principles, and consider the potential influence of
                                                                                                                                      contextual factors when planning and monitoring training loads.

                                                                                                                                      Key words: training load, injury, conceptual model, research methods, risk of bias




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.




                                                                                                                                                                                                                            2
                                                                                                                                       Introduction: a self-fulfilling prophecy

                                                                                                                                      “We must be careful not to believe things simply because we want them to be true, no
                                                                                                                                      one can fool you as easily as you can fool yourself“
                                                                                                                                                                                                    Richard Feymann

                                                                                                                                      It is tempting to believe a theory when it appears reasonable and it fits with one’s
                                                                                                                                      beliefs. For example, the theory that training “too much” or “too little”, or “too much
                                                                                                                                      too soon” might cause sports injury seems biologically plausible and aligns well with
                                                                                                                                      training dogma. Common beliefs about how training load affects the chances of the
                                                                                                                                      athlete getting injured have been strongly shaped by a combination of old and deeply-
                                                                                                                                      held training principles, best practice and common sense. Progressive overload, as
                                                                                                                                      well as the ‘danger’ of excessive training (overtraining or non-functional
                                                                                                                                      overreaching) are well-recognized training principles. The idea that excessive training




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      can increase injury risk can be traced back to early 1990s.44

                                                                                                                                      Popular beliefs about training load and injury obfuscate important concepts and
                                                                                                                                      methodological issues. Unfortunately, these issues have not been well accounted for
                                                                                                                                      in previous research. Our concern is that the training load and injury research field is
                                                                                                                                      dominated by well-intentioned, yet potentially misleading, recommendations for
                                                                                                                                      clinical practice.

                                                                                                                                      Collecting injury and training load data is now considered best practice in sport.14 An
                                                                                                                                      unfortunate consequence of such a data rich environment is that researchers studying




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      the relationship between training load and injury may retrospectively select from a
                                                                                                                                      convenient sample of available data rather than developing clear and well-defined
                                                                                                                                      research questions before collecting data. There are many studies reporting
                                                                                                                                      associations between training load and injury. The problem is, without a clear
                                                                                                                                      conceptual framework, it is easier for confirmation bias or selective reporting to creep
                                                                                                                                      in and hijack the truth.

                                                                                                                                      Clinicians are exposed to an ocean of information. One challenge for clinicians is to
                                                                                                                                      unravel the “signal” from the “noise” and identify relevant findings that can be
                                                                                                                                      confidently applied in practice. Most clinicians do not possess the ability to identify




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                      studies at high risk of bias, as this requires in depth research methods training. The
                                                                                                                                      aims of our clinical commentary are to (1) help clinicians identify some of the
                                                                                                                                      methodological weaknesses in training–load injury studies, and (2) demonstrate why
                                                                                                                                      clinicians should exercise caution when applying findings from these studies to their
                                                                                                                                      practice.

                                                                                                                                      Clinical question

                                                                                                                                      Is the methodological rigour of studies investigating relationships between training
                                                                                                                                      load and injury sufficient to inform training load-related decisions in clinical practice?
                                                                                                                                      We have highlighted why it is important to critically examine the strength of evidence
                                                                                                                                      supporting the claims made in several training load-injury studies.36 In this clinical
                                                                                                                                      commentary , we focus on sources of degrees of freedom that can favour questionable
                                                                                                                                      research practices (including p-hacking and HARK-ing (Hypothesizing After the
                                                                                                                                      Results are Known)) that can impact on the trustworthiness of research findings and
                                                                                                                                      the application of training load metrics in clinical practice.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 3
                                                                                                                                       A robust conceptual framework: the first step in designing quality research to
                                                                                                                                      help clinicians and athletes

                                                                                                                                      Developing a conceptual framework is an essential early step when designing
                                                                                                                                      research to inform clinical practice. If properly developed, a conceptual framework
                                                                                                                                      can guide researchers’ hypotheses and specific research questions, and provide a
                                                                                                                                      frame for analyzing data and interpreting the results.34 54 HARK-ing is a bit like doing
                                                                                                                                      research in reverse. When (well-intentioned) researchers do not develop a clear
                                                                                                                                      conceptual framework before collecting research data, they risk fashioning a
                                                                                                                                      hypothesis to suit their research results, and the temptation to conduct (unplanned)
                                                                                                                                      analyses until they find something “significant” (p-hacking).

                                                                                                                                      There have been attempts within the training load injury field to provide generic




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      concept maps and models.62 These can help clinicians understand the multifactorial
                                                                                                                                      nature of injuries and contextual factors that influence injury, but they lack detail to
                                                                                                                                      define precise research questions and/or select specific training load metrics. This
                                                                                                                                      necessitates the use of plausible biological and physiological rationale to select
                                                                                                                                      specific training load measures of exposure as potential prognostic factors for certain
                                                                                                                                      injuries. The conceptual framework proposed by Bertelsen et al.,6 is the most
                                                                                                                                      appropriate model of the causes of running-related injury (Figure 1).41 While one can
                                                                                                                                      argue the suitability of specific proxy measures (e.g. the use of ratios, or 7 and 28
                                                                                                                                      days cumulative load), we applaud the authors for transparently presenting their
                                                                                                                                      research assumptions, and encourage researchers to consider using the framework6 as




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      a starting point for new projects.42

                                                                                                                                      ***Figure 1****

                                                                                                                                      Conceptual frameworks must be verified (or disproven) through specific study of the
                                                                                                                                      hypothesized relationships between variables in the framework. If the hypotheses are
                                                                                                                                      confirmed by original studies, the model can be accepted as a reasonable explanation
                                                                                                                                      of the relationships. If the hypotheses are not confirmed, the researchers must go back
                                                                                                                                      to the drawing board and re-think their hypotheses. Research must challenge the
                                                                                                                                      assumptions and logic inherent to the framework to test its strength. Without a




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                      conceptual framework and predefined hypothesis about the relationship between
                                                                                                                                      variables, there is a risk of confirmation bias as the researchers may attempt to assign
                                                                                                                                      meaning to results.

                                                                                                                                      Without understanding and testing underlying etiology using a framework, it is
                                                                                                                                      impossible - irrespective of statistical approach - to accurately interpret research
                                                                                                                                      results. A satirical study in American Football55 illustrated that the risk of concussion
                                                                                                                                      was linked to the team logo: Teams with animal logos were protected from
                                                                                                                                      concussion. Should teams consider changing their logos or implementing ‘protective’
                                                                                                                                      animal stickers on their equipment to reduce the concussion risk?

                                                                                                                                      We expect most clinicians would agree that changing a logo is unlikely to change
                                                                                                                                      concussion risk. This article illustrates how, in the absence of a strong physiological
                                                                                                                                      rationale (i.e. framework), coincidental links may be misconstrued as clinical (or
                                                                                                                                      practical) recommendations. Our concern is that in absence of an established


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                4
                                                                                                                                       conceptual framework, the link between training load and sports injury might be
                                                                                                                                      misleading clinicians in sports science and medicine practice.

                                                                                                                                      A fishing expedition: p-hacking

                                                                                                                                      Many studies have reported associations between training load and sports injuries.
                                                                                                                                      However, the results are inconsistent and often confusing.17 We summarised the
                                                                                                                                      results (odd ratio (OR), relative risk (RR), and injury risk) of studies in soccer that
                                                                                                                                      calculated the ACWR from in-season session rating of perceived exertion (sRPE) or
                                                                                                                                      Global Positioning System (GPS) measures for non-contact injuries (Figure 2, Figure
                                                                                                                                      3). Some studies have reported a relationship between high ACWR and injury, some
                                                                                                                                      have reported a relationship between low ACWR and injury, and others have reported
                                                                                                                                      no relationship between ACWR and injury.




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      Using session RPE, three studies19 46 47 reported increased injury risk when the ACWR
                                                                                                                                      was high (Figure 2).4 In one study,39 the results were the opposite: a lower injury risk
                                                                                                                                      when the ACWR was high (Figure 2). In another study,16 there was no relationship
                                                                                                                                      between ACWR and injury injury 8 out of of 9 comparisons. For GPS-derived
                                                                                                                                      measures (figure 3), in one study there was no relationship between ACWR and injury
                                                                                                                                      risk in 4 out of 5 comparisons,10 elevated injury risk at high ACWR for total distance
                                                                                                                                      and accelerations but not for high speed distance and decelerations,9 and higher odd
                                                                                                                                      ratios for high-speed running, but not accelerations and decelerations.39 Confused? It
                                                                                                                                      is difficult to reconcile the inconsistencies to a cogent statement about the relationship
                                                                                                                                      between training load and injury. And these inconsistencies are not limited to studies




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      in soccer, or the ACWR metric.


                                                                                                                                      When one considers all of the relationships between all of the variables in all of the
                                                                                                                                      studies, what stands out is that some results might have been emphasized and others
                                                                                                                                      received little (or no) discussion – in research methods, this is referred to as selective
                                                                                                                                      reporting bias. The researcher emphasises the results that fit with his or her
                                                                                                                                      preconceptions, or the common beliefs about training load. For example, emphasizing
                                                                                                                                      three studies that supported a protective effect of moderate ACWR, and omitting
                                                                                                                                      other studies that did not show the same trend.21 Selective reporting (and discussion)




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                      of study findings misleads clinicians and researchers.

                                                                                                                                      *** Figure 2 ***

                                                                                                                                      *** Figure 3 ***

                                                                                                                                      Inconsistency between and within studies in the training load–injury field, is often
                                                                                                                                      justified by the multifactorial nature of injury etiology. While this is true and models
                                                                                                                                      accounting for this complexity have been proposed,8 32 33 the multifactorial nature of
                                                                                                                                      injury cannot be used as an excuse to ignore inconsistency. Instead, the complexity
                                                                                                                                      must be overcome with robust studies. A small number of training load metrics cannot
                                                                                                                                      adequately explain injury risk in sport.

                                                                                                                                      According to the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and
                                                                                                                                      Evaluation (GRADE) guidelines, inconsistency in the results of similar studies is
                                                                                                                                      grounds to downgrade the credibility of evidence.22 We recommend that researchers

                                                                                                                                                                                                                               5
                                                                                                                                       and practitioners examine all the results of the studies, avoiding or recognizing
                                                                                                                                      selective discussion. Be on the alert for implausible and inconsistent findings (also
                                                                                                                                      called unexpected associations), which may suggest associations due to chance,
                                                                                                                                      misclassification of the predictor, selection bias, mixing of effects (confounding),
                                                                                                                                      intervention effects and heterogeneity.53

                                                                                                                                      The decisions researchers make affect the likelihood of HARK-ing and p-
                                                                                                                                      hacking: threats to the credibility of results in the training load–injury field

                                                                                                                                      We believe the training load–injury field is at high risk of ‘data fishing’ – where
                                                                                                                                      researchers go searching (consciously or unconsciously) for answers in the data to
                                                                                                                                      confirm a relationship between training load and injury. Clinicians trying to apply
                                                                                                                                      research findings in practice may not be aware of all of the choices researchers must
                                                                                                                                      make when conducting a study, and how each choice might influence the results.




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      Sometimes, the choices researchers make might lead to false discoveries that favour
                                                                                                                                      their beliefs (confirmation bias). In this section, we highlight 8 methods issues
                                                                                                                                      (choices to be made by the researcher) that can increase the risk of p-hacking and
                                                                                                                                      HARKing (‘data fishing’).

                                                                                                                                      i) Measures of exposure and ratios
                                                                                                                                      In the absence of a strong a-priori conceptual framework, researchers are free to select
                                                                                                                                      the training load metric(s) they wish to include in a statistical model after the data are
                                                                                                                                      collected. Because there are so many different measures of training load (exposure),35




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      different researchers might make different choices. How does one interpret different
                                                                                                                                      results and different metrics, especially when there is a high chance of false
                                                                                                                                      discoveries? Different training load metrics may also have different relationships to
                                                                                                                                      injury risk.9 10 39

                                                                                                                                      Common measures of exposure (e.g. acute and chronic training load, and their ratio)
                                                                                                                                      lack conceptual and computational validity.38 56 Ratio measures of training load are
                                                                                                                                      common in the training load–injury field. However, the dangers of using ratios (as
                                                                                                                                      normalization method or dependent/independent variables) have previously been
                                                                                                                                      described, and the pitfalls well documented.3 15 58 When clinicians and researchers




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                      ignore warnings about using ratios as the main training load measure, they risk falsly
                                                                                                                                      concluding that the quantity of training load causes injury.

                                                                                                                                      ii) Training load measures
                                                                                                                                      Measures of exposure are calculated using various training load metrics. However,
                                                                                                                                      training load can be assessed using different methods and devices, which further
                                                                                                                                      complicates the selection of suitable measures. Again, a conceptual framework
                                                                                                                                      should provide guidance when selecting appropriate training load measures.
                                                                                                                                      Although studies have used sRPE, GPS, and inertial sensors, each of these measure
                                                                                                                                      different training load constructs.9 10 Therefore, combining injury rates from different
                                                                                                                                      sports and training load measures7 is inappropriate.

                                                                                                                                      iii) Time windows
                                                                                                                                       Without a conceptual framework it is not possible to justify what is an appropriate
                                                                                                                                      time window within which to measure acute load, and what is an appropriate time
                                                                                                                                      window within which to measure chronic load. The original Banister model cannot

                                                                                                                                                                                                                               6
                                                                                                                                       and should not be used to derive these time windows because the time decays used in
                                                                                                                                      the model are conceptually very different than weekly average training load. The
                                                                                                                                      solution to trial several windows concurrently (to find the best model)11 is prone to
                                                                                                                                      bias, multiple testing concerns and overfitting.

                                                                                                                                      iv) Time lags
                                                                                                                                      Typical time lags between injury registration and the acute or chronic load typically
                                                                                                                                      range from few days to one week (subsequent week injuries)11 29 31 40 but longer lags
                                                                                                                                      have been used.40 59 There is no reason to expect that the training completed on the
                                                                                                                                      day or days before an injury would not affect injury risk. Researchers do not usually
                                                                                                                                      explain why they chose a particular time lag over another time lag, raising suspicion
                                                                                                                                      of p-hacking.

                                                                                                                                      v) Discretization and reference category




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      Most studies lump training load measures and ratios into categories (Figure 2, Figure
                                                                                                                                      3). Such an approach has serious limitations,1 5 12 including that the number of
                                                                                                                                      categories can influence the results and subsequent interpretation. Using categories
                                                                                                                                      exacerbates the risks and consequences of sparse data bias (some categories have
                                                                                                                                      many data points, some categories have very few data points). Results from studies
                                                                                                                                      using different categories and references should not be compared.

                                                                                                                                      vi) Statistical analysis
                                                                                                                                      Most studies examining the association between training load and injury have used
                                                                                                                                      inadequate statistical analyses,49 61 including approaches that cannot account for time-




Downloaded from www.jospt.org at Ohio State University on August 10, 2020. For personal use only. No other uses without permission.
                                                                                                                                      varying variables, recurrent events or repeated measures.29-31 The challenges and
                                                                                                                                      solutions for more appropriate analysis have been provided, but are rarely followed.2
                                                                                                                                      49 50 52
                                                                                                                                               This is a problem because inappropriate analysis can produce unreliable and
                                                                                                                                      biased results.57

                                                                                                                                      vii) Missing data
                                                                                                                                      Missing training load data are common and sometimes unavoidable. Most studies in
                                                                                                                                      the training load–injury field do not descibe how missing data were handled. For
                                                                                                                                      example, were data imputed? What were the assumptions the researchers made about
                                                                                                                                      the missing data?24 57 Imputation can have an effect on the results. Sensitivity analyses




Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
                                                                                                                                      should be performed to show the effects of the methods, as recommended by
                                                                                                                                      international guidelines.13

                                                                                                                                      viii) Injury definitions
                                                                                                                                      The injury definition a researcher chooses is important. Some definitions are very
                                                                                                                                      broad (e.g. all complaints); others are narrow (e.g. serious, non-contact, time loss
                                                                                                                                      injuries). When researchers do not provide an appropriate rationale, grounded in a
                                                                                                                                      solid theoretical framework and etiology model, to justify their choice, it is difficult
                                                                                                                                      for readers to interpret results and compare studies. 23

                                                                                                                                      Correlation does not equal causation

                                                                                                                                      The dominant narrative of the training load–injury field is that by manipulating
                                                                                                                                      training load, one can alter the probability of future injuries. However, this assumes a
                                                                                                                                      cause-effect relationship (changing training load causes an injury to occur or not to


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 7
                                                                                                                                       occur) that has never been examined using appropriate methods required to make
                                                                                                                                      causal inferences.20 26 51 52

                                                                                                                                      Although the field acknowledged that association is not prediction,19 25 28 48
                                                                                                                                      (associations between training load metrics and injury do not automatically imply that
                                                                                                                                      training load metric can predict injury occurrence) – it is important to recognize that
                                                                                                                                      neither associations nor predictors can be automatically used to make causal
                                                                                                                                      inferences if this was not the original aim.27 Associations can be descriptive,
                                                                                                                                      predictive or used to estimate causal effects. However, if no causal relationship has
                                                                                                                                      been estimated, any practical applications regarding the manipulation of the
                                                                                                                                      prognostic factor/predictor to alter the probability of an event is an over interpretation
                                                                                                                                      and a speculation (and should be declared as such).

                                                                                                                                      Changing a risk factor like a training load metric, if the metric does not have a causal




Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
                                                                                                                                      relationship to the outcome or event, cannot modify the risk of an event occuring.
                                                                                                                                      Clinicians should be aware that, regardless the methodological approach, if the a
                                                                                                                                      study did not explicitly estimate causal effects (using appropriate methods), it is
                                                                                                                                      difficult to know whether changing training load causes injury. Ultimately, it should
                                                                                                                                      not be claimed that the intervention is “evidence-based” as often stated.

                                                                                                                                      Summary

                                                                                                                                      As published research in the training load-injury field has proliferated, clinicians
                                                                                                                                      might have been lulled into a false sense of security – accepting that training “too

                                                                                                                                      Recommendations for clinical practice

                                                                                                                                      Given the research limitations, we encourage clinicians to follow well-established

                                                                                                                                      training principles.43 45 One key principle is load progression. While some might
                                                                                                                                      believe that the current influx of studies have increased the attention to “correct
                                                                                                                                      handling “ of training load, this seems to be another bias. The overload progression
                                                                                                                                      concept has been well-known among coaches, fitness trainers and sport scientists for
                                                                                                                                      at least the past half-century (training and periodization principles); but we concede
                                                                                                                                      this may not be the case for clinicians who may not be as familiar with athletic
                                                                                                                                      training methods. Stronger multidisciplinary collaboration may help when making
                                                                                                                                      decisions about future training. We recommend clinicians work together with the
                                                                                                                                      various support staff of athletes/teams so that any specific knowledge and expertise is
                                                                                                                                      shared.

                                                                                                                                      When reading research in the training load–injury field, be on the look out for
                                                                                                                                      inconsistent results (“consistent” associations but in any direction is not a consistent
                                                                                                                                      finding) and different analysis methods that are not well justified (e.g. computational
                                                                                                                                      manipulations of the same prognostic factors, data trimming, categorizations, etc).

66	    Training load (TL) is a modifiable risk factor that may provide practitioners with opportunities to mitigate                             Accepted 23 April 2021

68	                                                                                                                                             KEYWORDS

224	Procedures
225	Familiarization
226	Prior to data collection, subjects were given a familiarization
227	period of one week which consisted of 3 separate education
228	sessions on the 0–10 Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale
229	(Foster et al., 2001). Additionally, subjects completed a yo-yo
230	intermittent test in order to anchor the top end of the RPE scale
231	and help establish accurate RPE scores for exercise intensity
232	(Gearhart, 2008). As this is a maximal test, subjects were
233	instructed afterwards that their last run should equate to the
234	highest score in the RPE scale.
235	
236	Training load data collection

238	a competitive match and two rest/recovery days. The composi­

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                                 ARTICLE HISTORY
    Training load (TL) is a modifiable risk factor that may provide practitioners with opportunities to mitigate                             Accepted 23 April 2021
    injury risk and increase sports performance. A regular problem encountered by practitioners, however, is
                                                                                                                                             KEYWORDS
    the issue of missing TL data. The purpose of this study was to examine the impact of missing TL data in                                  Training load; missing data;
    team sports and to offer a practical and effective method of missing value imputation (MVI) to address                                   team sports; injury;
    this. Session rating of perceived exertion (sRPE) data from 10 male professional soccer players (age,                                    performance
    24.8 ± 5.0 years; height, 181.2 ± 5.1 cm; mass, 78.7 ± 6.4 kg) were collected over a 32-week season. Data
    were randomly removed at a range of 5–50% in increments of 5% and data were imputed using 12 MVI
    methods. Performance was measured using the normalized root-mean-square error and mean of abso­
    lute deviations. The best-fitting MVI method across all levels of missingness was Daily Team Mean
    (DTMean). Not addressing missing sRPE data may lead to more inaccurate calculations of other TL metrics
    (e.g., acute chronic workload ratio, training monotony, training strain). The DTMean MVI method may
    provide practitioners with a practical and effective approach to addressing the negative consequences of
    missing TL data.

Subjects
Ten male professional soccer players volunteered to take part
in the study (age, 24.8 ± 5.0 years; height, 181.2 ± 5.1 cm; mass,
78.7 ± 6.4 kg). All players were contracted and played for the
senior first team, competing in the Premier League of Ireland.
All subjects were informed of the benefits and risks of partici­
pating, and written informed consent was completed before
undertaking the data collection in compliance with the
Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval for this research was
provided by the Institutional Research Ethics Review Board.


Procedures
Familiarization
Prior to data collection, subjects were given a familiarization
period of one week which consisted of 3 separate education
sessions on the 0–10 Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale
(Foster et al., 2001). Additionally, subjects completed a yo-yo
intermittent test in order to anchor the top end of the RPE scale
and help establish accurate RPE scores for exercise intensity
(Gearhart, 2008). As this is a maximal test, subjects were
instructed afterwards that their last run should equate to the
highest score in the RPE scale.

Training load data collection
A typical training week consisted of four team training days,
a competitive match and two rest/recovery days. The composi­
tion of training days varied but consisted of fitness condition­
ing, skill specific training, tactics and match preparation,
resistance training, speed and agility training and conditioned
games. Internal TL was calculated using the sRPE method as
described by Foster et al. (2001) (RPE x session duration in
minutes). sRPE has been shown to be a very common, practical,
reliable and valid method of measuring internal TL across
a wide variety of exercise modalities including soccer (Chen

15	Abstract
16	Causal pathways between training loads and the mechanisms of tissue damage and athletic injury are poorly understood.
17	Here, the relation between specific training load measures and metrics, and causal pathways of gradual onset and traumatic
18	injury are examined. Currently, a wide variety of internal and external training load measures and metrics exist, with many
19	of these being commonly utilized to evaluate injury risk. These measures and metrics can conceptually be related to athletic
20	injury through the mechanical load-response pathway, the psycho-physiological load-response pathway, or both. However, the
21	contributions of these pathways to injury vary. Importantly, tissue fatigue damage and trauma through the mechanical load-
22	response pathway is poorly understood. Furthermore, considerable challenges in quantifying this pathway exist within applied
23	settings, evidenced by a notable absence of validation between current training load measures and tissue-level mechanical
24	loads. Within this context, the accurate quantification of mechanical loads holds considerable importance for the estimation
25	of tissue damage and the development of more thorough understandings of injury risk. Despite internal load measures of
26	psycho-physiological load speculatively being conceptually linked to athletic injury through training intensity and the effects
27	of psycho-physiological fatigue, these measures are likely too far removed from injury causation to provide meaningful, reli-
28	able relationships with injury. Finally, we used a common training load metric as a case study to show how the absence of a
29	sound conceptual rationale and spurious links to causal mechanisms can disclose the weaknesses of candidate measures as
30	tools for altering the likelihood of injuries, aiding the future development of more refined injury risk assessment methods.

125	Training load             Training load is the term used by sports scientists, trainers, and athletes as the input variable that is manipulated to
126	                            elicit a desired training response in athletes. Within this context, load is a generic term which is qualified by the
127	                            term training in a fashion similar to other areas of research that have adopted the term load within a variety of con-
128	                            texts (i.e., allostatic load, cognitive load, mechanical load, etc.). Accordingly, training load does not specifically
129	                            refer to the forces experienced, as is typical in physics, or any other physical quantity. Training load, as a generic
130	                            construct, accommodates a variety of proxy measures and metrics (spatio-temporal, mechanical, psycho-physio-
131	                            logical, etc.) which can be described as being external or internal depending on whether the measurable aspect in
132	                            question is internal or external to the athlete. See below for explanations of terms external and internal
133	External (training) load  In the context of training load, the term external load implicitly refers to the external training load undertaken by an
134	                            athlete. External load has been defined as the physical work prescribed in the training plan (physical performance
135	                            output). Notably, this does not refer to ‘work’ in the physics sense (force × distance) but more so in a generic
136	                            manner. Accordingly, the term external load accommodates quantification and prescription in variety of manners,
137	                            enabling the use of a diverse range of external load measures and metrics. Some common measures of external
138	                            load include GPS derived units (e.g., speed, accelerations, etc.) and level of resistance
139	Internal (training) load  As per external load, the term internal load implicitly refers to internal training loads. In the context of training
140	                            load, internal load typically refers to the psycho-physiological stress experienced by an athlete. Notably, in this
141	                            context internal load does not describe the forces or internal stresses and strains experienced by specific biologi-
142	                            cal tissues. Rather, the concept of internal load incorporates all the psycho-physiological responses that an athlete
143	                            initiates to cope with the requirements elicited by the external load, irrespective of how the external load is quanti-

    REVIEW ARTICLE



Training Load and Injury: Causal Pathways and Future Directions
Judd T. Kalkhoven1          · Mark L. Watsford1 · Aaron J. Coutts1 · W. Brent Edwards2 · Franco M. Impellizzeri1

Accepted: 10 December 2020
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG part of Springer Nature 2020


Abstract
Causal pathways between training loads and the mechanisms of tissue damage and athletic injury are poorly understood.
Here, the relation between specific training load measures and metrics, and causal pathways of gradual onset and traumatic
injury are examined. Currently, a wide variety of internal and external training load measures and metrics exist, with many
of these being commonly utilized to evaluate injury risk. These measures and metrics can conceptually be related to athletic
injury through the mechanical load-response pathway, the psycho-physiological load-response pathway, or both. However, the
contributions of these pathways to injury vary. Importantly, tissue fatigue damage and trauma through the mechanical load-
response pathway is poorly understood. Furthermore, considerable challenges in quantifying this pathway exist within applied
settings, evidenced by a notable absence of validation between current training load measures and tissue-level mechanical
loads. Within this context, the accurate quantification of mechanical loads holds considerable importance for the estimation
of tissue damage and the development of more thorough understandings of injury risk. Despite internal load measures of
psycho-physiological load speculatively being conceptually linked to athletic injury through training intensity and the effects
of psycho-physiological fatigue, these measures are likely too far removed from injury causation to provide meaningful, reli-
able relationships with injury. Finally, we used a common training load metric as a case study to show how the absence of a
sound conceptual rationale and spurious links to causal mechanisms can disclose the weaknesses of candidate measures as
tools for altering the likelihood of injuries, aiding the future development of more refined injury risk assessment methods.
