Table 1  Relevant nomenclature
Operational definitions

Training load             Training load is the term used by sports scientists, trainers, and athletes as the input variable that is manipulated to
                            elicit a desired training response in athletes. Within this context, load is a generic term which is qualified by the
                            term training in a fashion similar to other areas of research that have adopted the term load within a variety of con-
                            texts (i.e., allostatic load, cognitive load, mechanical load, etc.). Accordingly, training load does not specifically
                            refer to the forces experienced, as is typical in physics, or any other physical quantity. Training load, as a generic
                            construct, accommodates a variety of proxy measures and metrics (spatio-temporal, mechanical, psycho-physio-
                            logical, etc.) which can be described as being external or internal depending on whether the measurable aspect in
                            question is internal or external to the athlete. See below for explanations of terms external and internal
External (training) load  In the context of training load, the term external load implicitly refers to the external training load undertaken by an
                            athlete. External load has been defined as the physical work prescribed in the training plan (physical performance
                            output). Notably, this does not refer to ‘work’ in the physics sense (force × distance) but more so in a generic
                            manner. Accordingly, the term external load accommodates quantification and prescription in variety of manners,
                            enabling the use of a diverse range of external load measures and metrics. Some common measures of external
                            load include GPS derived units (e.g., speed, accelerations, etc.) and level of resistance
Internal (training) load  As per external load, the term internal load implicitly refers to internal training loads. In the context of training
                            load, internal load typically refers to the psycho-physiological stress experienced by an athlete. Notably, in this
                            context internal load does not describe the forces or internal stresses and strains experienced by specific biologi-
                            cal tissues. Rather, the concept of internal load incorporates all the psycho-physiological responses that an athlete
                            initiates to cope with the requirements elicited by the external load, irrespective of how the external load is quanti-
                            fied. For examples of internal load please see "psycho-physiological load" below.
Psycho-physiological load Refers to the psycho-physiological stress experienced by an athlete in response to a given external load. A range of
                            physiological and psycho-physiological measures and metrics exist, with common physiological measures being
                            heart rate, blood lactate etc. and a common psycho-physiological measure being rating of perceived exertion
                            (RPE). The psycho-physiological stress experienced is considered to contribute substantially to the training out-
                            come that presents. Notably, the value and validity of specific training load indicators depends on the context. For
                            example, heart rate is a valid measure of internal load for endurance training but not so much for resistance training
Mechanical load           Refers to the forces experienced by specific tissues or biological structures and can be externally or internally
                            sourced e.g., collision with an opponent or muscle pulling on bone. The mechanical load is the stimulus that
                            results in the mechanical load-response (stress and strain)
Stress                    Stress is defined as force per unit area and develops within a structure/tissue in response to externally applied
                            mechanical loads (force). Stress is descriptive of the internal forces neighbouring particles of a given material exert

Strain                    Refers to the amount of deformation expressed as a normalized change in shape or size. Two basic types of strain

                            mal strain is the ratio of deformation (lengthening or shortening) to original length and as such may be tensile or
                            compressive. Shear strain is the amount of angular deformation that occurs in a structure. For example, a rectangle

 "evidenceSummary":"Narrative review of how training load may relate to tissue damage and injury through mechanical and psycho-physiological load-response pathways. The authors use the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) as a case study and report conceptual flaws in its inputs and inconsistent associations with injury across studies. No new data were analysed.",
 "screeningLimitations":"No systematic search or pooled analysis is described, so the conclusions rest on the authors' reading of the literature. The mechanical load pathway is acknowledged to be hard to measure in applied settings, so the review offers no tested replacement metrics.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read this as showing that training load has no role in injury, when the paper's claim is that current metrics and their causal links are poorly supported.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Kalkhoven JT, Watsford ML, Coutts AJ, Edwards WB, Impellizzeri FM. Training Load and Injury: Causal Pathways and Future Directions. Sports Med. 2020.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-020-01413-6",
   "abstract":"The review examines causal pathways from training load to tissue damage and athletic injury through mechanical and psycho-physiological load-response pathways. It uses the acute:chronic workload ratio as a case study of a metric with weak conceptual foundations. The authors conclude that current training load measures are poorly linked to injury causation.",
   "tldr":"Current training load metrics have weak links to the causes of injury, so they should not be used to assess injury risk or to change training as an injury-reduction measure. Training load data remain useful for checking that athletes complete what is prescribed.",
   "methods":"Narrative review of mechanical fatigue and tissue damage literature, internal and external load measures, and the conceptual basis of the acute:chronic workload ratio. No systematic search method is described and no new data were analysed.",
   "findings":"The authors argue that the mechanical load-response pathway is poorly quantified in applied settings and that GPS and accelerometer proxies are weakly related to tissue-level loads. They state that psycho-physiological internal load measures such as RPE are too far removed from injury causation to show reliable links with injury. They describe the ACWR as having conceptual flaws, including interchangeable inputs, a protective role assumed for chronic load, and acute windows justified by convenience, and they note that its associations with injury point in contradictory directions.",
   "limitations":"This is a conceptual review, so it does not quantify effect sizes or test the proposed pathways. The authors acknowledge that tissue-level loading cannot be measured in the field, which limits the practical alternatives they can offer.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use training load data mainly to confirm that athletes are doing what was prescribed and how they are coping with it. Do not base injury risk decisions, or training changes made to reduce injury, on the ACWR or similar metrics unless a causal link has been tested.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance work, use training load data to monitor whether athletes complete the prescribed work and how they cope with it. Do not treat the ACWR or similar ratios as evidence that a load change will reduce injury risk.",
   "rtp":"Does not directly inform return to sport. It argues against using training load metrics to judge injury risk and gives no return-to-play criteria, so it should not be used to set return-to-play thresholds."
 }
}

No new data are reported and no systematic search method is described.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The framework is proposed by the authors and is not tested against athlete data, and the response-rate example is hypothetical. The biomechanical pathway is supported mainly by theory, because accelerometer and GPS measures are only loosely related to tissue loading.",

   "abstract":"The authors propose a framework that treats physiological and biomechanical load-adaptation pathways separately in running-based team sports. They revisit the distinction between internal and external load and review GPS, accelerometer and internal load evidence. They suggest that the two pathways respond at different rates, which affects how training and rehabilitation should be sequenced.",
   "tldr":"Team sport monitoring mostly tracks physiological load, while tissue (biomechanical) load is largely overlooked. Separating the two pathways may help sequence training and rehabilitation, but the framework still needs testing.",

They state that the mechanical load-adaptation pathway has been largely overlooked and that tissue adaptation is slower than physiological adaptation, which may call for different periodization of physiological and biomechanical load. Examples include aqua jogging and anti-gravity treadmill running to reduce biomechanical load, and maximal sprints on sand, which carry high physiological load with lower impact.",

The authors note that current accelerometer and GPS measures are only loosely related to tissue loads, which limits how the biomechanical pathway can be measured.",
   "practicalImplications":"When planning sessions, consider physiological and biomechanical demand separately, for example by using lower-impact work when tissue load needs reducing.    "athleteDev":"For performance planning, separate physiological and biomechanical load when sequencing sessions, and consider lower-impact options such as sprints on sand when tissue load needs reducing. Treat the framework as a hypothesis, since it has not been tested.",

 }
}

   "abstract":"This secondary analysis of 32 weeks of daily sRPE data from 10 male professional soccer players removed 5-50% of values at random. Daily team mean imputation was the most accurate method at all missingness levels.",
   "tldr":"When sRPE data are missing, imputing the day's team mean was the most accurate of the methods tested and is simple to apply. Errors grow as missingness increases, so the first priority is keeping missing data low.",
   "methods":"Complete sRPE data (RPE multiplied by session minutes) from 10 male professional soccer players over a 32-week season were used, with 5-50% of values removed at random in 5% steps. Twelve imputation methods were scored against the observed values using NRMSE and MAD.",
   "findings":"Daily Team Mean had the lowest NRMSE (0.42-0.46) across all missingness levels, and player-based methods were less accurate (NRMSE 0.48-0.68).    "practicalImplications":"Keep sRPE missingness as low as possible, for example by giving players regular feedback that their data are used. If missingness exceeds about 10%, review the monitoring process, as the authors suggest.",
   "athleteDev":"For squad load monitoring, fill missing sRPE with the day's team mean before calculating ACWR, monotony or strain, and keep missingness low. Use this approach for squad-based data, not for individual programmes.",
   "rtp":"Not designed for return to sport. The method relies on the team mean, which the authors say should not be used for players in post-injury rehabilitation, so it should not be applied to returning players."
